newsitem.title: CANADA: British Columbia sets job creation plan for forests.
newsitem.headline: British Columbia sets job creation plan for forests.

text.p: British Columbia unveiled plans on Thursday to increase employment in its forestry industry by 25 percent over the next four years, in what the province called one of Canada's biggest job creation efforts.

Premier Glen Clark told a news conference in this community about 500 miles (804.7 km) north of Vancouver that the so-called Jobs and Timber Accord called for the creation of 39,800 jobs to be created by 2001.
Industry analysts said it remained to be seen if the ambitious targets could be achieved and many details of the program had yet to be worked out.

Dave Haggard, president of the IWA-Canada lumber workers union, hailed the plan, saying union workers had "faced downsizing to no end. Now finally I'm standing here and listening to a government that listened to the people."
British Columbia will spend C$1.9 billion ($1.4 billion) in total or C$370 million ($267 million) a year on the program.

The announcement followed more than a year of tough talks between the government and forestry company presidents, many of whom resisted Clark's effort. The industry pressed for relief from government bureaucracy and high regulatory costs in exchange for backing the plan.
The industry, the backbone of British Columbia's economy accounts for about a third of gross domestic product but has been hit by high costs and lagging profitablity.
Industry analysts estimated 5,500 jobs were lost in the province's forest sector last year. The government put current direct employment at 86,000 workers.
The accord will be closely scrutinized by U.S. lumber producers, who are on the lookout for anything than can be seen as a subsidy to their Canadian competitors.
British Comumbia hopes to avoid upsetting the U.S. lumber lobby little more than a year after Canada and the United States signed a trade deal resolving a dispute over lumber.
